questions.question: What are Maven's three built-in lifecycles?
questions.title: Maven's Three Lifecycles
questions.direct_answer: Maven has three built-in lifecycles: default (handles project build and deployment), clean (removes build output), and site (generates project documentation). Each lifecycle is independent and consists of a sequence of phases.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Maven's lifecycle model beyond just the default lifecycle phases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing the default lifecycle and thinking 'clean' is just a phase, not a separate lifecycle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 'mvn clean package' invokes TWO lifecycles — clean first, then default up to package — showing you understand lifecycle independence

sections.title: Maven's Three Independent Lifecycles
sections.content:
Maven organizes build operations into three completely independent lifecycles, each designed for a specific purpose. Think of them like separate assembly lines in a factory — each has its own sequence of steps, and they don't interfere with each other.

The **default lifecycle** is the workhorse that handles compiling code, running tests, packaging artifacts, and deploying them. The **clean lifecycle** is a simple two-phase process (pre-clean and clean) that removes all build artifacts from the target directory, giving you a fresh start. The **site lifecycle** generates project documentation, reports, and a website from your source code and configuration. When you run a Maven command like 'mvn clean package', you're actually invoking two lifecycles sequentially: clean runs first to wipe out old artifacts, then default runs up to the package phase. Understanding this independence is crucial because it explains why 'mvn clean' doesn't automatically trigger a build, and why 'mvn package' doesn't automatically clean first unless you explicitly combine them.

sections.content:

blue|clean|~Remove output|pre-clean, clean|deletes target/|fresh start
emerald|site|~Documentation|reports + website|rarely used daily|generated from config

sections.title: Running Maven Lifecycles in Practice
sections.content:
```xml
// pom.xml for a Spring Boot multi-module project
<project>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>
  
  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-clean-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.0</version>
        <!-- clean lifecycle uses this plugin -->
      </plugin>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        <!-- default lifecycle's package phase uses this -->
      </plugin>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-site-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.12.1</version>
        <!-- site lifecycle uses this plugin -->
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>

// Command line examples
// Runs ONLY clean lifecycle
$ mvn clean

// Runs ONLY default lifecycle up to package phase
$ mvn package

// Runs clean lifecycle, THEN default lifecycle up to install
$ mvn clean install

// Runs ONLY site lifecycle
$ mvn site
```

sections.title: When to Use Each Lifecycle
sections.content:
Use the **default lifecycle** (via commands like mvn compile, mvn test, mvn package) for all normal development work — building your application, running tests, creating JAR or WAR files. This is what you'll use 90% of the time.

Use the **clean lifecycle** (mvn clean) before important builds to ensure no leftover compiled classes or artifacts from previous builds are interfering, especially when switching branches or troubleshooting weird build behavior. Combine them as 'mvn clean package' for release builds or when you want absolute certainty about a fresh build.

Use the **site lifecycle** (mvn site) when you need to generate project documentation or reports for stakeholders, though this is less common in day-to-day development. Most freshers will work primarily with default and occasionally with clean.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking clean is just a phase**: Many freshers believe 'clean' is just another phase in the default lifecycle like compile or test, when it's actually a completely separate lifecycle with its own phases. This causes confusion about why 'mvn package' doesn't automatically clean first.
- **Running clean every single time**: Some developers get into the habit of always running 'mvn clean package' even for quick iterative development, which wastes time because clean deletes everything and forces a full rebuild from scratch. During active development, just run 'mvn package' unless you're troubleshooting strange issues.
- **Ignoring the site lifecycle**: Freshers often don't know the site lifecycle exists at all, missing an opportunity to generate useful project documentation and reports automatically from your codebase and Maven configuration.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three lifecycles**: default (build), clean (remove artifacts), site (documentation) — each is completely independent
- **Lifecycle independence**: Running one lifecycle doesn't trigger another; 'mvn clean package' explicitly invokes both clean then default
- **Default lifecycle**: The main workhorse with phases like compile, test, package, install, deploy for building and distributing artifacts
- **Clean lifecycle**: Simple two-phase lifecycle (pre-clean, clean) that deletes the target directory to remove all build output
- **Site lifecycle**: Generates project documentation, reports, and websites from source code and Maven configuration
- **Command syntax**: You invoke a lifecycle by naming a phase; Maven runs all earlier phases in that lifecycle automatically
- **Practical usage**: Combine lifecycles explicitly when needed like 'mvn clean install' to ensure a fresh build before installing to local repository

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven has three built-in lifecycles that are completely independent of each other. The default lifecycle is the main one you use for building projects — it includes all the phases like compile, test, package, install, and deploy. The clean lifecycle is simpler, it just has two phases that remove all the build output from your target directory. And the site lifecycle generates project documentation and reports. The key thing to understand is that these lifecycles don't automatically trigger each other. When you run a command like mvn clean package, you're actually telling Maven to run two separate lifecycles in sequence. First it runs the clean lifecycle to wipe out old artifacts, then it runs the default lifecycle up to the package phase. This is different from phases within a lifecycle, where running a later phase automatically runs all the earlier ones. For example, if you just run mvn package without clean, Maven won't delete your target directory first — it'll just run the default lifecycle phases leading up to package. In real development work, you'll use the default lifecycle constantly for building and testing. You'll combine it with clean when you want to be absolutely sure you have a fresh build, like when you're switching Git branches or investigating weird build issues. The site lifecycle is less common, mostly used when you need to generate documentation for stakeholders or create project reports.

questions.question: What are the key phases of Maven's default lifecycle in order?
questions.title: Maven Default Lifecycle Phases
questions.direct_answer: The key phases in order are: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy. Each phase executes automatically when you invoke any later phase — for example, mvn package runs validate, compile, and test before packaging.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Maven knowledge — knowing the lifecycle order is essential for understanding what happens during any Maven command
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that install puts the artifact in the local ~/.m2 repository, not that it deploys to a production server
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between install (local repo) and deploy (remote repo) clearly, showing you understand artifact distribution

sections.title: Understanding Maven's Default Lifecycle Phases
sections.content:
Maven's default lifecycle is a sequence of phases that execute in a strict order, and each phase depends on all previous phases completing successfully.

Think of it like a manufacturing assembly line where each station must complete its work before the product moves to the next station. When you invoke any phase like 'mvn package', Maven automatically runs all the earlier phases first — you don't need to explicitly run compile or test separately. This design ensures consistency: you can't accidentally package code that hasn't been compiled or tested. The **validate** phase checks that the project is correct and all necessary information is available. The **compile** phase compiles source code into bytecode. The **test** phase runs unit tests against the compiled code. The **package** phase bundles the compiled code into distributable format like JAR or WAR. The **verify** phase runs integration tests and checks to verify the package is valid. The **install** phase copies the artifact to your local Maven repository (~/.m2) so other local projects can use it. Finally, **deploy** uploads the artifact to a remote shared repository for team-wide access. Understanding this sequence is fundamental to working with Maven effectively.

sections.title: mvn package Triggers Every Earlier Phase
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[validate] --> C[compile] --> T[test] --> P[package] --> Ve[verify] --> I[install] --> D[deploy]
```

sections.title: Maven Default Lifecycle in a Spring Boot Project
When to Use Each Phase
sections.content:
Use **mvn compile** during active development to quickly check if your code compiles without running tests — useful when you're making rapid changes and just want syntax validation.

Use **mvn test** when you want to run unit tests but don't need to create a JAR file yet, common during test-driven development cycles.

Use **mvn package** as your standard build command for creating deployable artifacts — this is what you'll use most often, as it compiles, tests, and packages everything.

Use **mvn verify** when you have integration tests configured (usually with maven-failsafe-plugin) and want to run both unit and integration tests.

Use **mvn install** when you're working on a multi-module project and one module depends on another, so you need the artifact in your local ~/.m2 repository for other modules to reference.

Use **mvn deploy** only in CI/CD pipelines or when you need to share your artifact with the team via a remote repository like Nexus or Artifactory — never use this casually during development.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Running phases individually**: Freshers often run 'mvn compile' then 'mvn test' then 'mvn package' as three separate commands, not realizing that 'mvn package' automatically runs compile and test first. This wastes time and shows a misunderstanding of how phases work.
- **Confusing install with deployment**: Many freshers think 'mvn install' deploys their application to a server. It actually just copies the JAR to your local ~/.m2/repository directory so other Maven projects on your machine can use it as a dependency. Deploying to a server is done by tools like Docker or Kubernetes, not Maven install.
- **Skipping to package without understanding**: Running 'mvn package' without understanding that it's running tests underneath can be dangerous. If tests fail, the build fails — some freshers then disable tests entirely rather than fixing the failing test, which defeats the purpose of automated testing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Phase order**: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy, always executed in sequence
- **Automatic execution**: Running any phase automatically runs all earlier phases; mvn package runs validate, compile, and test first
- **Compile phase**: Converts Java source files (src/main/java) into bytecode (.class files) in target/classes directory
- **Test phase**: Executes unit tests using maven-surefire-plugin; build fails if any test fails unless you skip tests explicitly
- **Package phase**: Bundles compiled code into JAR or WAR based on packaging element in pom.xml
- **Install vs deploy**: install copies to local ~/.m2 repository for your machine only; deploy uploads to remote shared repository for team access
- **Verify phase**: Often overlooked, this runs integration tests with maven-failsafe-plugin after packaging but before install

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key phases of Maven's default lifecycle in order are validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy. The important thing to understand is that when you run any phase, Maven automatically runs all the earlier phases first. So if I run mvn package, Maven doesn't just package my code — it first validates the project, then compiles the source code, then compiles and runs the unit tests, and only then creates the JAR or WAR file. This automatic sequencing is really powerful because it ensures you can't accidentally create a package from code that hasn't been tested. The compile phase takes your Java source files from src slash main slash java and turns them into class files in the target directory. The test phase runs your JUnit tests, and if any test fails, the whole build fails right there. The package phase creates your JAR or WAR file in the target directory. After package comes verify, which is where integration tests run if you have them configured. Then install copies that JAR to your local dot m2 repository, which is at tilde slash dot m2 slash repository on your machine. This is really useful in multi-module projects where one module needs to use another as a dependency. Finally, deploy uploads the artifact to a remote Maven repository like Nexus or Artifactory so your whole team can access it. A common mistake freshers make is thinking install deploys the app to a server, but it actually just installs it to your local Maven repo. Deploying to actual servers is done by different tools.

questions.title: Common Maven Commands

sections.title: Essential Maven Commands for Daily Development
sections.content:
Maven commands are how you interact with Maven's build lifecycle and plugins from the command line. Each command invokes specific lifecycle phases or plugin goals. The commands you'll use daily fall into two categories: lifecycle phase commands that build your project, and plugin goal commands that perform specific tasks like analyzing dependencies or generating reports. **mvn clean** removes all build artifacts from the target directory, giving you a fresh start. **mvn compile** compiles your source code but doesn't run tests or package. **mvn test** compiles and runs unit tests. **mvn package** does everything up to creating a JAR or WAR file. **mvn install** additionally copies that artifact to your local Maven repository. **mvn clean package** combines two operations: cleaning first, then packaging. Understanding these commands is essential because you'll type them dozens of times per day.

The key insight is that most commands trigger a chain of earlier phases automatically, so you rarely need to run multiple commands sequentially. One analogy: think of Maven commands like ordering at a restaurant — when you order the full meal (package), you automatically get the appetizer (compile) and main course (test) without having to order them separately.

amber|clean / compile|~Reset or build classes|deletes target/|javac to classes|quick checks
blue|test / package|~Verify then bundle|runs JUnit|creates JAR or WAR|package runs both first
emerald|install / deploy|~Share the artifact|install to ~/.m2|deploy to a remote repo|for other projects
violet|dependency:tree|~Diagnose deps|a plugin goal, not a phase|shows transitives|debug conflicts

sections.title: Common Maven Commands with Output
When to Use Each Command
sections.content:
Use **mvn compile** when you're actively coding and want quick feedback that your code compiles without waiting for tests to run — common during rapid iteration on new features.

Use **mvn test** when you're doing test-driven development and want to run tests repeatedly without creating a JAR each time.

Use **mvn package** as your default build command when you want to create a deployable artifact — this is what you'll use most often, it's the standard "build my project" command.

Use **mvn clean package** before important demos, releases, or when troubleshooting mysterious build issues, because it guarantees a completely fresh build with no leftover artifacts.

Use **mvn install** when working on multi-module projects where module A depends on module B, so you need B installed in your local repository for A to compile.

Use **mvn dependency:tree** when you're debugging dependency conflicts or trying to understand why a particular transitive dependency is being pulled in — this is a crucial troubleshooting command that many freshers don't know.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Running unnecessary sequential commands**: Freshers often run mvn compile, then mvn test, then mvn package as three separate commands, not realizing that mvn package automatically runs compile and test. This wastes time and shows you don't understand Maven's phase chaining. Just run mvn package once.
- **Always using clean**: Some developers habitually run mvn clean package every single time, even during rapid development iterations. Clean deletes everything and forces a full rebuild from scratch, which is slow. During active development, just use mvn package — Maven's incremental compilation is smart enough to only recompile what changed.
- **Not knowing diagnostic commands**: Many freshers only know the basic build commands and don't know about mvn dependency:tree for debugging dependency issues, or mvn versions:display-dependency-updates to check for outdated dependencies. Learning these diagnostic commands makes you much more effective at troubleshooting real problems.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **mvn clean**: Deletes target directory to remove all compiled classes and build artifacts for a fresh start
- **mvn compile**: Compiles src/main/java source code to target/classes but doesn't run tests or create JAR
- **mvn test**: Compiles and runs unit tests with maven-surefire-plugin; build fails if any test fails
- **mvn package**: Most common command, runs validate through package phases to create JAR or WAR in target directory
- **mvn install**: Runs all phases through install, copying artifact to ~/.m2/repository for use by other local projects
- **mvn clean package**: Combines two operations — removes old artifacts first, then runs full build; use before releases or when troubleshooting
- **mvn dependency:tree**: Plugin goal (not lifecycle phase) that displays dependency tree including transitive dependencies, essential for debugging conflicts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The most commonly used Maven commands are mvn clean, mvn compile, mvn test, mvn package, mvn install, and mvn clean package. Let me explain what each does. Clean removes the target directory where all your compiled code and build artifacts live, so you start fresh. Compile just compiles your Java source code into class files but doesn't run tests or create a JAR. Test compiles your code and runs your unit tests — if any test fails, the build stops right there. Package is probably the command you'll use most often because it does everything: compiles your code, runs your tests, and then creates a JAR or WAR file in the target directory. Install takes it one step further by copying that JAR to your local dot m2 repository, which is useful when you're working on multi-module projects where one module depends on another. And clean package combines clean and package into one command, which is what you use before important builds to make absolutely sure there's no leftover artifacts from previous builds that could cause problems. One really important thing that trips up freshers is that you don't need to run these commands sequentially. If you run mvn package, Maven automatically runs compile and test first because those are earlier phases in the lifecycle. You don't need to type mvn compile then mvn test then mvn package as three separate commands. A bonus command that shows you know your stuff is mvn dependency colon tree. This isn't a lifecycle phase, it's a plugin goal that displays your entire dependency tree including all the transitive dependencies. This is super useful when you're debugging dependency conflicts or trying to figure out where a specific JAR is coming from.

questions.question: How do you skip tests in Maven and when is it appropriate?
questions.title: Skipping Tests in Maven
questions.direct_answer: Use mvn package -DskipTests to skip test execution but still compile tests, or -Dmaven.test.skip=true to skip both compilation and execution. It's appropriate only in specific scenarios like emergency hotfixes, investigating non-test build failures, or CI pipeline debugging — never as regular practice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Maven knowledge plus professional judgment about when skipping tests is acceptable
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always skipping tests as a habit to make builds faster — this defeats the purpose of automated testing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between -DskipTests (compiles tests but doesn't run them) vs -Dmaven.test.skip=true (skips compilation too), showing nuanced understanding

sections.title: Understanding Test Skipping Options in Maven
sections.content:
Maven provides two ways to skip tests, each with different implications for the build process. The flag **-DskipTests** tells Maven to compile your test classes but not execute them — the maven-surefire-plugin still runs, but it skips the actual test execution. The flag **-Dmaven.test.skip=true** goes further and tells Maven to skip both test compilation and execution entirely — your test source files aren't even looked at. Understanding the distinction matters because skipping compilation saves more time but means you won't catch syntax errors in your test code.

Think of it like skipping a safety inspection: -DskipTests is like running the inspection but not fixing the issues found, while -Dmaven.test.skip=true is like not even showing up for the inspection. Both are dangerous if used carelessly. In professional development, tests exist to catch bugs before they reach production. Skipping them should be a rare, deliberate decision with clear justification, not a habit to make builds faster. The only legitimate scenarios are emergency hotfixes where tests are known to pass, investigating build infrastructure issues unrelated to tests, or debugging CI/CD pipeline problems where you need to isolate variables.

sections.title: Skipping Tests
sections.content:
amber|-DskipTests|~Skip execution|still compiles tests|catches test syntax|the safer choice
blue|-Dmaven.test.skip|~Skip compile too|no test code touched|maximum speed|riskier
emerald|Legit uses|~Rare + deliberate|emergency hotfix|build-infra debugging|CI isolation
rose|Anti-pattern|~Never a habit|hides real bugs|fix slow tests instead|tell the team if shared

sections.title: Skipping Tests the Right Way
sections.content:
```bash
# Skip test EXECUTION, but still compile test classes (safer)
mvn package -DskipTests

# Skip BOTH test compilation and execution (faster, riskier)
mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true

# Better than skipping everything: run just the test you care about
mvn test -Dtest=OrderServiceTest
```

sections.title: Step 1: Assess Your Specific Situation
sections.content: Before skipping tests, honestly assess why you want to do it. If it's because tests are failing and you want to get a build out anyway, that's exactly the wrong reason — those failing tests are catching real problems. Legitimate reasons include: you're investigating a build problem that happens before tests even run (like a compilation error in main code), you're debugging a CI/CD pipeline configuration issue and need to isolate whether the problem is in the build itself or the test execution, or you're doing an emergency production hotfix where you've manually verified the fix works and are in time-critical mode. If you're skipping tests just to make builds faster during normal development, that's a red flag. Fast feedback is valuable, but not at the cost of knowing your code works. In that case, the right solution is to improve your test suite's performance, not skip the tests.

sections.title: Step 2: Choose the Appropriate Skip Flag
sections.content: If you've determined skipping tests is justified, choose the right flag. Use **-DskipTests** when you want to skip test execution but still want Maven to compile your test code. This is safer because you'll still catch compilation errors in your test classes. Use this when investigating runtime issues or when you need a quick build but want to maintain some level of test code validation. Use **-Dmaven.test.skip=true** only when you need maximum speed and you're certain your test code doesn't have compilation issues. This skips both test compilation and execution, saving more time but giving you zero feedback about your test code. The syntax matters: -DskipTests is a property recognized by maven-surefire-plugin specifically, while maven.test.skip is a broader Maven property that affects both the compiler and surefire plugins. In practice, -DskipTests is the safer default choice for the rare times you need to skip tests.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making it a habit**: The biggest mistake is adding -DskipTests to your regular development workflow to make builds faster. This completely defeats the purpose of automated testing — you're essentially flying blind, not knowing if your changes broke anything. Tests exist to give you confidence that your code works; skipping them means you've lost that confidence.
- **Skipping tests for failing builds**: When tests fail and a deadline is looming, freshers often skip tests to get a build out. This is exactly backwards — failing tests are telling you there's a problem. Shipping code with known test failures is how bugs reach production.
- **Not communicating with the team**: In a team setting, if you skip tests to push code to a shared branch or deploy to a shared environment, other developers have no idea that untested code is now in the codebase. This can cause confusion when they pull your changes and find bugs. Always communicate when you're doing something non-standard like skipping tests, and document why in your commit message or deployment notes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **-DskipTests flag**: Compiles test classes but skips test execution; maven-surefire-plugin runs but doesn't execute tests
- **-Dmaven.test.skip=true**: Skips both test compilation and execution; no test code is touched at all, saves maximum time
- **Command syntax**: mvn package -DskipTests or mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true, property flags go after the phase name
- **Legitimate use cases**: Emergency hotfixes, investigating non-test build failures, CI/CD pipeline debugging — all temporary situations
- **Never make it a habit**: Skipping tests to make builds faster defeats automated testing; fix slow tests instead
- **Team communication**: If you skip tests on shared branches, communicate why and document it in commit messages
- **Production risk**: Code deployed without tests passing has higher risk of bugs reaching users; only acceptable in genuine emergencies

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are two ways to skip tests in Maven, and they're slightly different. You can use mvn package with the flag dash D skipTests, which tells Maven to compile your test code but not actually run the tests. Or you can use dash D maven dot test dot skip equals true, which skips both compiling and running the tests. The difference is that dash D skipTests is safer because it still compiles your test code, so you'll catch any syntax errors in your tests. The other flag skips tests completely and saves more time but gives you zero feedback about whether your test code even compiles. Now here's the important part about when it's appropriate to skip tests. The short answer is almost never during normal development. Tests exist to catch bugs before they reach production, and skipping them means you're deploying code without knowing if it works. But there are a few legitimate scenarios. If you're doing an emergency hotfix and you've manually verified the fix works and you're in time-critical mode, you might skip tests to save a couple minutes. If you're investigating a build problem that happens before tests even run, like a compilation error in your main code, you might skip tests to isolate the issue. Or if you're debugging a CI/CD pipeline configuration, you might skip tests to figure out if the problem is in the build process or the test execution. But these are all temporary, specific situations. The biggest mistake freshers make is habitually adding dash D skipTests to their builds to make them faster. That defeats the entire purpose of automated testing. If your tests are slow, the solution is to optimize them, not skip them.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'mvn install' and 'mvn deploy'?
questions.title: mvn install vs mvn deploy
questions.direct_answer: mvn install copies the packaged artifact to your local ~/.m2 repository on your machine so other local projects can use it as a dependency. mvn deploy uploads the artifact to a shared remote Maven repository like Nexus or Artifactory for the entire team and CI/CD system to access.

sections.title: Install vs Deploy: Local and Remote Artifact Distribution
sections.content:
The confusion between install and deploy is one of the most common misunderstandings among Java freshers, because the word "deploy" has two completely different meanings in software development. In Maven, both commands are about distributing your built JAR or WAR file to repositories where other projects can reference it as a dependency, but they target different repositories for different purposes. **mvn install** takes your packaged artifact and copies it to your local Maven repository, which is a directory on your machine at ~/.m2/repository (tilde slash dot m2 slash repository).

This is useful when you're working on multiple projects locally and one project needs to use another as a dependency. **mvn deploy** takes your artifact and uploads it to a remote Maven repository like Nexus, Artifactory, or Maven Central. This shared repository is accessible to your entire development team, CI/CD pipelines, and production systems. Think of install as putting your artifact in your personal desk drawer, while deploy is putting it in a shared filing cabinet that the whole office can access. Critically, neither command has anything to do with deploying your application to a runtime server like Tomcat, Kubernetes, or AWS. That kind of deployment is done by completely different tools.

sections.title: install vs deploy in Practice
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- deploy needs a target repository; install needs nothing -->
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>company-releases</id>
    <url>https://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-releases/</url>
  </repository>
</distributionManagement>
```
`mvn install` copies the artifact to `~/.m2`; `mvn deploy` uploads it to the repository above for the whole team.

sections.title: Install vs Deploy Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | mvn install | mvn deploy |
|---|---|---|
| Target location | Local ~/.m2/repository directory | Remote shared Maven repository |
| Accessibility | Only your machine | Entire team and CI/CD systems |
| Primary use case | Multi-module local development | Sharing artifacts team-wide |
| Configuration needed | None, works out of box | Requires distributionManagement in pom.xml |
| When to use | Building dependent local modules | Publishing releases or snapshots |

sections.title: When to Use Install vs Deploy
sections.content:
Use **mvn install** when you're working on a multi-module Maven project on your local machine. For example, if you have an order-service module that depends on a common-utils module, you need to install common-utils to your local repository first so order-service can find it as a dependency. This is a daily activity during development — you make changes to common-utils, run mvn install, then rebuild order-service which picks up the updated version from your local repository.

Use **mvn deploy** in CI/CD pipelines or when you need to publish a release or snapshot version that your team can use. This is typically automated in your build pipeline — when you merge code to the main branch, the CI system runs mvn deploy to push the artifact to your shared Nexus or Artifactory repository. Then other developers or services can pull that version as a dependency. You rarely run mvn deploy manually from your local machine unless you're the release manager publishing an official version. The key distinction: install is for local development convenience, deploy is for team-wide artifact distribution.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking deploy means server deployment**: The most common mistake is thinking mvn deploy deploys your application to a runtime server like Tomcat, Kubernetes, or AWS. It doesn't — it only uploads your JAR to a Maven artifact repository. Deploying to servers is done by tools like Docker (docker push), Kubernetes (kubectl apply), or cloud deployment scripts. Maven deploy is purely about artifact repository management.
- **Running deploy during local development**: Some freshers run mvn deploy from their local machine during normal development, accidentally pushing snapshot versions to the shared repository. This pollutes the repository with unnecessary artifacts and can confuse teammates. Deploy should almost always happen in CI/CD pipelines, not local machines.
- **Not configuring distributionManagement**: Maven deploy requires a distributionManagement section in your pom.xml specifying the remote repository URL and credentials. Freshers often try to run mvn deploy without this configuration and get confused when it fails. If you're not sure whether your project is configured for deploy, it probably isn't, and you shouldn't be running it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **mvn install**: Copies artifact to local ~/.m2/repository on your machine for other local projects to reference as dependencies
- **mvn deploy**: Uploads artifact to remote shared Maven repository (Nexus, Artifactory) for team-wide access
- **Not application deployment**: Neither command deploys your app to servers; that's done by Docker, Kubernetes, or deployment scripts
- **Local development**: Use install daily when working on multi-module projects where modules depend on each other
- **Team sharing**: Use deploy in CI/CD pipelines to publish releases or snapshots for team consumption
- **Configuration requirement**: Deploy requires distributionManagement section in pom.xml with repository URL and credentials
- **Artifact repositories**: Nexus and Artifactory are enterprise Maven repository managers that host team artifacts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between mvn install and mvn deploy is about where your built artifact goes and who can access it. Install copies your JAR or WAR file to your local Maven repository, which is a directory on your machine at tilde slash dot m2 slash repository. This is really useful when you're working on multiple projects locally and one project depends on another. For example, if I'm building an order-service that depends on a common-utils library I'm also developing, I'll run mvn install on common-utils first to put it in my local repo, then when I build order-service it can find common-utils as a dependency right there on my machine. Deploy is different — it uploads your artifact to a remote Maven repository that's shared across your entire team, like Nexus or Artifactory. This is how you make your artifact available to other developers, CI/CD systems, and production environments. Typically deploy happens automatically in your CI/CD pipeline when you merge code. One really important thing that trips up freshers is the word deploy itself. In Maven, deploy doesn't mean deploying your application to a server like Tomcat or Kubernetes. It only means uploading your JAR to a Maven repository. Actually deploying your app to a runtime server is done by completely different tools like Docker, Kubernetes, or deployment scripts. Maven deploy is purely about artifact distribution, not application deployment. Another mistake is running mvn deploy from your local machine during development — you almost never want to do this because it pushes artifacts to the shared repository unnecessarily. Deploy should happen in CI/CD, not on your laptop.
